This model's dynamic component is based on a non-autonomous center manifold theorem that enables efficient estimation and facilitates the identification of time-varying patterns. Finally, we demonstrate the model's applicability through a simulation study and a real-world analysis of COVID-19 transmission data. This model offers a valuable tool for researchers seeking to analyze and model non-stationary Poisson time series.

The eigenvector method is a widely used technique to identify influential nodes within complex networks by taking into account the connectivity patterns of nearby nodes. This approach calculates a centrality score for each node based on a weighted sum of its connections' scores, resulting in a self-referential process that reflects the network's overall structure. Building on this foundation, we have developed a multilayer extension of the eigenvector method that considers both the connectivity of adjacent nodes across different layers and the inter-layer connections. This new approach enables the simultaneous analysis of node centrality across multiple layers, providing a comprehensive framework that can be applied to a broad range of real-world problems. We have also developed a numerical method to solve the system of equations arising from this approach, as well as a local iteration algorithm that can be used for large-scale networks. Furthermore, we have examined the multilayer eigenvector approach in comparison to existing methods through both synthetic and real-world network data, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately identifying influential nodes across multiple layers. This approach has been applied to the analysis of node centrality in multilayer networks, revealing the complex dynamics of the 2008 global financial crisis, as well as the centrality of cities in a multilayer transportation network. This research has been made available as an R package called'mevn' for public use.

Cross-domain recommendation has been widely used in various applications, and it has been particularly successful in multi-sparse-domain scenarios. However, existing research often relies on the assumption that there is a significant overlap in user preferences across domains. In contrast, this study focuses on a more challenging problem with minimal inter-domain preference overlap, and it proposes a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that leverages a user's comprehensive aspect preferences to facilitate recommendation across multiple sparse domains. The integration of private electric vehicles into the power grid poses both opportunities and challenges. On one hand, they can provide a source of energy and enhance grid resilience. On the other hand, their charging patterns may compromise the stability of the grid. This research focuses on analyzing the effects of private electric vehicles on distribution network resilience and proposes a multi-agent optimization framework to manage their charging behavior. The study utilizes a multi-objective optimization approach to balance the benefits of energy supply and grid stability, and applies a non-dominant sorting genetic algorithm to solve the optimization problem. A case study is conducted to evaluate the proposed method, and the results indicate that a coordinated charging policy can significantly enhance grid resilience. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of considering the spatial distribution of private electric vehicles in urban areas when designing their charging management systems. Ultimately, the research demonstrates the value of a coordinated charging policy in promoting grid resilience and provides a framework for managing the impacts of private electric vehicles on distribution network resilience.

The context of an image significantly influences the accuracy of object detection
tasks, and the effectiveness of context has been extensively studied in recent years.
However, the impact of context on deep object detectors in relation to their
internal representations remains poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we
propose a novel method to assess the context's influence on object detectors by
utilizing their internal representations. Specifically, we employ a contrastive loss to
learn a context-aware representation that distinguishes between relevant context and
irrelevant background. The effectiveness of this representation serves as an indicator
of the context's influence on the object detectors. We evaluate our method on three
benchmarks, including the COCO dataset, and find that it accurately captures the
context's influence on object detectors. Furthermore, we leverage this assessment
method to investigate the context's influence on object detectors and deep neural
networks, revealing interesting insights. Our code is publicly available at
https://github.com/zhengyangyin/Context-Assessment.

The study also investigates the applicability of WBW to Single Input Single Carrier OFDM (SISO-OFDM) and Single Input Multiple Carrier OFDM (SIMC-OFDM) systems. To accelerate policy optimization in complex tasks, experience replay has been widely utilized to speed up training by reducing the need for simultaneous interaction with the environment. However, the effectiveness of experience replay is compromised when combined with policy optimization methods that rely on variance to guide their search for better policies. This is because the distribution of sampled transitions from the replay buffer can be skewed, leading to suboptimal policy updates. To address this limitation, we introduce a Variance Diminution based Experience Replay (VDER) framework that modifies the replay buffer distribution to match a target distribution aligned with policy optimization objectives. We demonstrate the VDER framework's versatility in incorporating various distribution alignment methods, including a novel approach that leverages policy-based reweighting. Our experiments with challenging tasks, such as robotic manipulation and 3D cube navigation, show that VDER significantly improves policy optimization by reducing variance in the replay buffer and promoting more informed policy updates. Our findings also reveal that VDER's performance can be further enhanced by selecting suitable distribution alignment methods and hyperparameters. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuchen/VDER.

We analyzed the recurrence patterns of 21 known neutron star transient systems within the Milky Way, and found that the distribution of recurrence intervals for 13 systems with known orbital periods did not differ from those with unknown periods. However, for the 8 systems with known orbital periods, the distribution of recurrence intervals was bimodal, with peaks at approximately 70-90 days and 160-200 days. We also proposed a method for identifying transient systems with short orbital periods in other crowded regions, like globular clusters and the Large Magellanic Cloud. In Federated Learning, sensitive data remains with individual users, ensuring the privacy of their information. However, this approach is limited to a single organization that trains a model jointly with its employees, and extending it to multiple organizations with a central server, known as Vertical FL, poses significant privacy challenges. Although privacy-enhancing techniques like secure multi-party computation and FL can address this issue, they come with substantial computational costs and reduced model accuracy. In this research, we explore the vulnerabilities of a widely adopted, privacy-preserving VFL method and demonstrate how a malicious server can launch a series of attacks to compromise the privacy of users in a real-world scenario. Furthermore, we propose a new attack strategy that can circumvent the limitations of existing privacy-preserving VFL methods and provide a computational framework for the server to launch a privacy assault on users. Additionally, we conduct experiments to evaluate the impact of this attack on the model's performance and the costs associated with it. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the need for enhanced privacy-preserving VFL methods to safeguard user data in real-world applications.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective for a wide range of machine learning tasks, yet the computational costs associated with the large number of kernel matrix evaluations make them less than ideal for large-scale applications. To address this limitation, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate the kernel matrix via a computationally efficient dot product in a hyperspace of lower dimension. This method relies on a fixed number of random features that is independent of the size of the dataset. In contrast, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the inherent information present within the data to determine an optimal set of features, resulting in an approximation that outperforms traditional methods by a significant margin. Experimental evaluations across multiple classification and regression tasks demonstrate the improved performance of our method, as well as its ability to yield a 10-fold reduction in the number of features required compared to standard RFF. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the proposed method's theoretical properties, establishing a non-asymptotic error bound for the kernel approximation and demonstrating the consistency of the resulting estimator. The implementation of our method, along with the theoretical guarantees and experimental results, are made readily available to the public.

A marked ordered tree is defined as an ordered tree where each node has a designated left or right child. Researchers have been studying the properties of marked ordered trees to gain insights into various stochastic processes. In this study, we examine the structure of marked ordered trees through the concept of deepest vertices. A deepest vertex is the farthest node from the root, considering the distance along the tree's edges. We calculate the expected number of deepest vertices in a marked ordered tree of $n$ nodes and derive its probability distribution. Additionally, we investigate the conditions under which there are two, one, or no deepest vertices. The analysis yields expressions for the number of deepest vertices as $E[\text{ndes}(T_n)] = 2 - 2/h_n$ and its probability distribution as $\text{ndes}(T_n) \stackrel{d}{=} \lfloor 2h_{n-1} \rfloor$. The study also explores the relationship between marked ordered trees and Yule processes, enabling the derivation of an explicit formula for the expected number of deepest vertices in a Yule process as $E[\text{ndes}(Y_t)] = 2 - 2e^{-2t}$. The research provides a new perspective on marked ordered trees and offers a solution to a problem posed by Aldous in 1990. The findings can be applied to the study of coalescent processes and population genetics. The integrity of democratic processes heavily relies on the accuracy of election results, which are often determined by counting paper ballots. To ensure the reliability of these outcomes, it is crucial to conduct thorough investigations of the counting process and the ballot tabulation system. This research presents a novel approach called Informed Optical Character Identification (iOCR) that enables the rapid and efficient comparison of scanned ballot tally sheets by automatically detecting discrepancies in the scanned text. The iOCR system was tested on a large dataset of over 1.5 million scanned entries from the 2020 US presidential election in Georgia, achieving a 99.98% accuracy rate in identifying differences. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the feasibility of applying the iOCR system to investigate the integrity of the ballot counting process and provides a framework for future research in this area. The iOCR system is made available to the public for use in similar investigations of democratic processes.

Deep neural networks have achieved superior performance in various computer vision tasks due to the availability of vast amounts of data. However, the current paradigm is challenged by the emergence of new classes in tasks with a massive number of predefined classes, such as ImageNet. Traditional methods that rely on pre-trained models with a fixed number of classes face difficulties when encountering unknown classes. In contrast, end-to-end deep learning methods can adapt to new classes but are hindered by the requirement for a massive amount of data to be effective. In this work, we present a novel dynamic learning framework that overcomes the limitations of both approaches. By introducing a class-activation based dynamic graph neural network, our method is able to selectively focus on a subset of samples that are relevant to the new classes, thereby achieving superior performance with a significantly reduced number of data. Experimental results on CUB, PLACES, and a subset of ImageNet demonstrate the superiority of our approach. Furthermore, we extend our method to tackle the multi-label classification problem on ImageNet, achieving a new state-of-the-art performance of 83.4% top-1 accuracy on a 1 million-class dataset with only 1000 classes. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangyin/dynamic-learning.

However, the underlying relationship between Neural ODEs and traditional neural networks remains poorly understood. This study delves into the connection between Neural ODEs and Hamiltonian Neural Networks, exploring how the latter can be used as a proxy to approximate derivatives. Through the use of Hamiltonian Neural Networks, we demonstrate the equivalence to Neural ODEs and reveal the network's ability to learn derivatives, even complex ones, through a series of experiments. Additionally, we uncover the connection between Neural ODEs and residual connections within the context of a simple example. Ultimately, our findings provide a novel perspective on Neural ODEs and offer a practical application for Hamiltonian Neural Networks in the computation of derivatives.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is a critical task in Natural Language Processing, 
where a word with multiple senses is identified within a given context. 
Traditionally, WSD has been approached using supervised machine learning methods, 
where a model is trained on labeled data to make predictions for new, 
unlabeled text. However, obtaining high-quality training data with labeled senses 
is extremely challenging and time-consuming. In response, researchers have explored 
semi-supervised methods, leveraging existing resources like Wikipedia and glossaries 
to supplement the limited labeled data. In this paper, we propose a novel approach 
to incorporate Wikipedia articles as context-gloss pairs to enhance WSD performance. 
Each Wikipedia article is treated as a context-gloss pair, where the article 
represents the context and the corresponding category title represents the gloss. 
We employ a BERT-based model to classify the senses based on the context-gloss 
pairs, and evaluate our method on the Senseval and SemEval datasets, achieving 
state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, we conduct an ablation study to examine the 
effectiveness of incorporating Wikipedia context-gloss pairs, and find that they 
are highly beneficial for training the model. Additionally, we investigate the 
optimal way to select Wikipedia articles for training and find that using articles 
with a single category title per page yields the best results. Finally, we 
demonstrate that our approach is adaptable to other WSD datasets and models, 
and that it can be applied to other NLP tasks, such as Named Entity Recognition. 
Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/ContextGlossEnhancement. 
Our approach surpasses the current state-of-the-art results on the Senseval and 
SemEval datasets, and our method is simple, efficient, and adaptable to various 
NLP tasks.

A significant challenge in zero-shot cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing lies in the lack of training data for target domains. To address this issue, researchers have employed the zero-shot approach, which relies on class-based parameters to facilitate parsing across various domains. However, this method requires an extensive dataset of text descriptions as additional input to generate execution plans. In contrast, a more efficient approach would directly generate execution plans from input SQL queries and raw text without the need for additional text descriptions. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel end-to-end framework that incorporates an auxiliary task to bridge the gap between domains. The proposed framework consists of an encoder that generates a unified representation from raw text and input SQL queries, and a decoder that produces execution plans. To facilitate cross-domain parsing, the encoder is trained to predict a domain-invariant code from the unified representation, and the decoder is trained to generate execution plans based on this code. The proposed framework is evaluated on Spider, demonstrating its effectiveness over the class-based approach. To further validate the proposed framework, we conduct an ablation study and analyze the impact of the auxiliary task on the encoder. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/chenxu1997/EndtoEndCrossDomainTSQL.

We introduce a novel method for efficiently computing the exact Most Probable Explanation (MPE) and constrained optimisation in graphical models, leveraging a compact representation of functions defined on variables within the models. This representation enables us to employ a range of existing algorithms for submodular function minimisation to solve two key problems efficiently. Specifically, we use it to derive a polynomial-time algorithm for calculating the exact MPE and another for constrained optimisation with a guaranteed polynomial time complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach can be applied to a wide range of graphical models, including Bayesian networks and Markov random fields, without requiring any modifications. Our method's efficacy is substantiated through experimental results, which show that it outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods for exact MPE calculation in many instances. Our algorithm's time complexity is also comparable to that of the most efficient approximate MPE algorithms. Our code is available online for public use.

This study examines the collider's capabilities to explore various theoretical frameworks, including the Higgs sector, electroweak symmetry breaking, dark matter, and extra dimensions. By utilizing state-of-the-art simulations, we evaluated the collider's potential to produce and detect key particles, such as dark photons, hidden Higgs bosons, and extra-dimensional gravitons, and assessed its sensitivity to new physics parameters. Our analysis indicates that a 1.2 TeV, 4 TeV-$c^2$ muon collider could detect the Higgs boson's unknown decay channels, reveal the composition of dark matter, and uncover extra dimensions, and that it would surpass the capabilities of existing and future particle colliders. Furthermore, we identified the most promising production and detection methods for various new physics scenarios and provided a comprehensive roadmap for future research and development. Our findings demonstrate that a TeV-scale muon collider offers unparalleled opportunities to explore the fundamental nature of the universe and would be an exceptionally powerful tool for advancing our understanding of the cosmos. Ultimately, we argue that such a collider should be considered as a vital component of the global particle physics research agenda.

Reconstructing 3D scenes from monocular images is a complex task, and estimating the 3D motion between frames is even more challenging. Despite the difficulty, a promising approach emerged in 2020, where researchers found that self-supervised learning could accurately predict 3D scene flows from a single image. Building upon this breakthrough, researchers have been exploring various methods to enhance the performance. However, most existing techniques focus on improving the network's capacity to capture general 3D features, neglecting the crucial role of scene geometry in 3D motion estimation. In contrast, our proposed method, which we call Adversarial Metric Learning for Self-Supervised Scene Flow Estimation (AML-SF), targets the most challenging scenarios with complex geometry and occlusions. AML-SF introduces a novel metric learning framework that leverages the network's ability to capture geometric information to generate scene flows with precise spatial structure. The proposed network is trained using a contrastive adversarial loss function that encourages the predicted scene flows to conform to a predefined motion graph, thereby capturing the intrinsic 3D geometry of the scene. The proposed AML-SF method achieves superior performance in estimating scene flows from a single image under self-supervised learning settings, surpassing the state-of-the-art methods on the SfS dataset by a significant margin. The method's versatility is further demonstrated by its successful application to the challenging KITTI dataset, where it achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art supervised learning methods. The proposed AML-SF method is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyin1995/Adversarial_Metric_Learning_SF. The code for training the network is written in PyTorch, and the pre-trained models for the SfS and KITTI datasets are provided in the supplementary materials. Modern cloud-native applications comprise numerous microservices running within containers, leading to a surge in system calls from containers. This growth poses a significant threat to the security of these systems. Current solutions either rely on system call monitoring across all containers or employ static policy configurations, which are either overly permissive or fail to account for changing service requirements. In contrast, our research introduces Timeloops, a novel approach that autonomously learns container system call policies based on observed behavior. This approach leverages a combination of machine learning algorithms and system call metadata to create a policy that can be applied to past, present, and future system call patterns. Our evaluation demonstrates a 2.5x reduction in allowed system calls compared to a baseline policy, while maintaining a 99% accuracy in predicting system calls for a real-world containerized application. Furthermore, Timeloops can be easily integrated into existing container runtime environments with minimal overhead. Our research provides a foundation for a more dynamic and adaptive approach to managing container system calls in cloud-native applications.

As a result, inferred measurements contain residual errors and biases that can be a major obstacle for many applications. Furthermore, we found that the PREPPI deconvolution technique can lead to biased inferred measurements due to the over-smoothing of small-scale features. To alleviate these biases, we applied a Gaussian filter to the inferred measurements before they are used in further analysis. A key challenge in training neural network models with non-local interactions, such as those found in Hubbard models, is the Hubbard sign problem. This issue arises when using real-valued optimizers to minimize the loss function, causing it to become non-differentiable and complicating stochastic gradient descent. To address this, we propose a novel method of reformulating the Hubbard interaction using complex-valued neural networks, which eliminates the sign problem and facilitates the use of real space discretization. By applying this approach to a neural network-based cellular automaton, we successfully simulated a one-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model and obtained accurate results for various parameters. Furthermore, our method allows for the use of a wide range of optimizers, including Adam and RMSProp, and enables the application of complex-valued neural networks to other models with local and non-local interactions. To facilitate the reproduction of our results, we have made our code publicly available.

Transfer learning is a common technique in deep learning where a pre-trained model is adapted for a new task with limited data. However, when the source and target tasks are dissimilar, performance can significantly decline. In unsupervised settings, cross-task generalization is an unaddressed issue, where the goal is to enhance a model's ability to perform on one task without receiving any supervision for another, unrelated task. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel unsupervised cross-task generalization framework that leverages unlabelled data from the target domain to improve performance on the source domain. Our approach employs a retrieval-based method to incorporate relevant target domain data that is similar to the source domain, thereby enabling the model to generalize more effectively. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on several unsupervised cross-task generalization benchmarks, showcasing improved performance over existing methods. Additionally, we apply our approach to enhance the robustness of deep neural networks in a real-world scenario, where the goal is to improve performance on one task without receiving any supervision for another, similar task. Our approach achieves superior results compared to baselines in this setting as well. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/RetCross.

Optimizing hyperparameters for deep learning models is a challenging task, especially when privacy constraints are applied. The introduction of differential privacy (DP) adds a new layer of complexity due to the trade-off it imposes between model accuracy and data privacy protection. This trade-off is further complicated by the need to consider multiple hyperparameters simultaneously. In this research, we develop a novel approach to efficiently optimize hyperparameters for private deep learning models in a single-shot manner. Our method, called Efficient Hyperparameter Optimization for Private Deep Learning (EHOPL), employs a meta-learning framework to determine the optimal hyperparameter configuration with minimal data, thus reducing the computational burden. EHOPL is subsequently used to guide a local search optimization algorithm for further refinement, enabling the exploration of a broader search space and facilitating the escape from local optima. We conduct extensive experiments on multiple private deep learning models and datasets, and the results demonstrate the superiority of EHOPL over traditional optimization methods, including Bayesian optimization and evolutionary algorithms. Furthermore, we provide insights into the interplay between hyperparameters, privacy levels, and model performance in the context of DP deep learning. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

However, existing solutions often prioritize simplicity over efficiency and fail to meet the performance requirements of large-scale periodic stream processing tasks. In our experiments, LifeStream demonstrated exceptional speedup and scalability, outperforming Spark Structured Streaming by up to 13x and Flink by up to 5x on a 16-node cluster. To facilitate further research, we have made LifeStream's source code publicly available.

Deep learning models have successfully integrated multiple sources of information to enhance speech recognition. However, the current state of end-to-end multi-modal models often relies on pre-trained vision and language representations, which can be inflexible and may not generalize well to new tasks. In contrast, a speech-text based approach that trains models on raw speech and text data has shown promise, but often overlooks the importance of directional information flow. To address these limitations, we propose a novel bidirectional focus mechanism to selectively utilize both forward and backward information in multi-modal models. This approach is particularly beneficial for training models on raw speech and text data. We evaluate our method on the Librispeech and Google's Wav2Text datasets, achieving significant improvements over the baseline. Specifically, we observe a 4.3% relative improvement in WER for the Librispeech "test-clean" set and a 6.4% relative improvement in WER for the Google's Wav2Text dataset. Our approach also demonstrates the effectiveness of bidirectional focus in multi-modal models, with a 2.5% relative improvement in WER for the Librispeech "test-clean" set when using pre-trained vision and language representations. Predicting future video frames from a given sequence has numerous practical
applications in fields such as robotics, self-driving cars, and video editing.
However, existing methods primarily focus on forecasting short-term frames
(less than 1 second) and struggle with longer-term predictions, especially for
complex and dynamic scenes. To address this challenge, a new approach is
proposed that utilizes a two-part learning framework to accurately forecast
video sequences over a second. Initially, a recurrent neural network is trained
to generate a compact, low-resolution video representation that captures the
overall scene dynamics. Next, a generative adversarial network is trained to
produce a high-resolution video based on this representation. To further
refine the model, a secondary network is trained to predict the residual between
the actual and predicted frames. This new method is tested on several video
prediction datasets and achieves superior results to existing methods for
predictions over a second. Source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-hu/new-view-prediction.

The metric dimension of a graph measures the minimum number of nodes required to identify all other nodes unambiguously based on their distances to the identifying nodes. We introduce a new parameter, the trimmed metric dimension, which removes nodes from the graph that can be unambiguously identified by existing nodes before considering the remaining subset. We establish lower and upper bounds for the trimmed metric dimension and show it is equivalent to a specific subgraph's dimension. We also investigate the trimmed metric dimension in specific graphs, including paths, cycles, and complete graphs. Furthermore, we examine the trimmed metric dimension in relation to the trimmed version of another well-known parameter, the location number. We then explore the trimmed metric dimension's properties in graphs with a central node and those without a node with degree greater than one. Lastly, we provide an algorithm to calculate the trimmed metric dimension and discuss its connection to the trimmed location number. We conclude by proposing several open research questions.

for understanding stellar evolution, particularly in relation to astrophysical 
processes such as mass loss, rotation, and pulsation. A significant challenge 
in this field is the scarcity of reliable data on close binary systems with 
main-sequence components, particularly those with orbital periods under two 
days. The discovery of binary Agermain variables, characterized by alternating 
brightness and color changes, can provide valuable insights into these systems. 
However, detecting these systems is difficult due to the limited sensitivity 
of current surveys. This study leverages the Pan-STARRS1 survey's extensive 
photometric data to develop a novel method for identifying binary Agermain 
variables. By applying this method to Pan-STARRS1 data spanning nearly a year, 
we created a comprehensive list of candidate binary Agermain variables. 
Subsequent observations using the Gemini-North telescope confirmed the 
binary nature of 13 out of 25 selected candidates. These newly discovered 
binary Agermain variables exhibit orbital periods ranging from 1.2 to 4.5 days 
and mass ratios between 0.3 and 0.8. This study's findings significantly 
expand the known population of binary Agermain variables and provide valuable 
information for future surveys searching for similar systems. 
Furthermore, we propose a method for identifying binary Agermain variables 
in current and future surveys, such as the LSST survey. 
This method involves analyzing the variability of stars with spectral types 
F-G and luminosity classes III-IV. 
We anticipate that this method will be particularly effective in discovering 
binary Agermain variables in the LSST survey.

for close binary systems with main-sequence components.

Proteins can form intricate knots within their three-dimensional structures, and these knots can resist unwinding under mechanical stress. Recent studies suggest that the paths these proteins take during folding are influenced by topological constraints, potentially favoring specific knot-bending pathways over others. However, pinpointing these pathways in knotted proteins proves to be a challenging task. We developed a statistical approach to identify preferred knot-bending pathways based on the three-dimensional structures of knotted proteins. This method was applied to proteins knotted in the shape of trefoil knots, allowing us to compare the predicted pathways with actual structures and determine that there are distinct preferred pathways. These pathways are influenced by the proteins' chemical properties and can be used to guide simulations of protein folding. Furthermore, we found that proteins with trefoil knots tend to favor pathways that involve the crossing 4$_{1}$-shift, a previously undiscovered pattern of movement. This shift is distinct from other known patterns and could be an essential feature of protein folding under topological constraints. This finding is supported by simulations of protein folding using a coarse-grained model. We also found that proteins with trefoil knots that have a knot that is more deeply embedded tend to favor pathways that involve the 4$_{1}$-shift more frequently than proteins with a less embedded knot. This discovery is significant because it provides a possible explanation for why some proteins with trefoil knots are more resistant to unwinding than others. This study demonstrates the importance of considering topological constraints when studying protein folding and the potential for cross-over between chemistry and topology in the folding of proteins with knots. This research also highlights the potential of statistical analysis of protein structures to reveal patterns of protein folding that are influenced by chemistry and topology. This study focused on proteins with trefoil knots, but the methods developed here can be applied to proteins with other types of knots. In this talk, we delve into the specifics of a Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem that deviates from its standard form, focusing on its peculiar characteristics. A particular class of symmetry breakings, where the shift in the symmetry and the resulting long-range force have opposite signs, serve as prime examples of this unusual phenomenon. We examine the conditions under which such unusual NG scenarios emerge, exploring both relativistic and non-relativistic contexts. Furthermore, we investigate the implications of these unusual NG scenarios on low-energy interactions and the associated low-energy effective field theories. Additionally, we discuss the relevance of these unusual NG scenarios to various physical systems, including those with spontaneously broken scale symmetry, certain types of super-symmetry breaking, and the Higgs phase of certain gauge theories. The primary function of conditional knowledge in conversational settings is
to facilitate the generation of hypothetical scenarios for evaluating
counterfactual statements. However, the current state of the art in conditional
knowledge lacks a clear understanding of its internal workings, particularly
regarding phrasal counterfactual conditions. In this paper, we introduce the term
"phrasal hypotheticals" to describe conditions consisting of two phrases that are
connected by a specific relation, which we aim to infer through a language
model. We propose a straightforward method to train a strong language model to
generate such conditions and assess its effectiveness using a new evaluation
metric, which we call the "hypothesis plausibility score". We also present a
method to fine-tune the pre-trained language model for the task of generating
counterfactual text, which we evaluate using a set of manually curated
counterfactual statements. Our results show that the proposed method yields
better performance compared to a strong baseline, which we demonstrate using the
hypothesis plausibility score. Our research provides a novel perspective on the
internal workings of conditional knowledge and offers practical applications
for generating counterfactual text. Our code is available at https://github.com/nyuclg/disco.

The proliferation of wearable devices has led to a significant increase in health-related data, which can be utilized to develop accurate and individualized machine learning models for healthcare. However, the data is typically generated on mobile devices and cannot be directly used due to privacy concerns. This issue is compounded by the limited amount of data available for training accurate models. To address this challenge, we propose FedHealth, a federated transfer knowledge framework that enables the secure and efficient development of personalized health models using wearable data across multiple devices. FedHealth leverages the benefits of federated learning to maintain user data privacy and employs a transfer knowledge approach to adapt models to individual users. We demonstrate the efficacy of FedHealth through comprehensive experiments using real-world data from the MIMIC-CXR dataset and wearable data from the PhysioNet dataset. The results show that FedHealth achieves superior performance compared to conventional machine learning models trained on individual devices. Furthermore, FedHealth exhibits robustness in adapting to new users and provides a user adaptation period that can be adjusted to balance performance and data transmission. The code for FedHealth is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wang/FedHealth.

This framework utilizes a hybrid indexing approach that balances the trade-offs between query speed and storage capacity. In noisy environments, speech processing systems face significant interference, necessitating effective noise reduction techniques. Deep learning models have shown significant promise in addressing this challenge, but they often require large amounts of clean data for training and can be computationally expensive. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) for single-channel speech enhancement. This novel network integrates convolutional and recurrent components in two separate paths to process spectral and temporal information. The convolutional path employs a spectral filter to adapt to non-linear spectral patterns, while the recurrent path utilizes a GRU to capture temporal dependencies. The two paths are then combined to produce the final enhanced spectrum. DPCRN is trained using a combination of adversarial and mean squared error criteria, resulting in a compact 1.4M parameter model. Experimental evaluations on the DNS challenge dataset demonstrate DPCRN's effectiveness, with a 3.34 dB improvement in short-term objective intelligibility and a 0.38% reduction in word error rate compared to the baseline. Additionally, DPCRN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of model size and computational requirements. Code for DPCRN is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-nyu/DPCRN.

The precise measurement of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is crucial for accurately determining the parameters of our universe. However, detecting these anisotropies is challenging due to the inherent noise and systematic errors in modern experiments. To effectively mitigate these issues, it's essential to simulate the instrumental biases of CMB observations. We present a Python package called s4cmb, designed to simulate the biases in modern CMB experiments for both spatial and spectral domains. Capable of modeling various instrumental characteristics, s4cmb can simulate data from experiments using both total power and correlation measurements. The package includes tools for visualizing and analyzing the simulated data, as well as a module for estimating the optimal window functions for the simulated experiments. We demonstrate the capabilities of s4cmb by simulating and analyzing the biases in the CMB-S4 experiment, which is expected to achieve high-precision measurements of the cosmic microwave background. By facilitating the simulation of instrumental biases, s4cmb can aid researchers in designing future CMB experiments and interpreting their data. The package is available on GitHub under the MIT license.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger formulated two problems related to angle spaces. An angle space is defined as a function $\Delta$ that maps pairs of distinct lines to real numbers in $[0,\pi]$ while satisfying certain properties, including the condition that for any line $l$ not equal to $m$ or $n$, the value of $\angle(l,m) + \angle(m,n) = \angle(l,n)$ is independent of the lines $l$, $m$, and $n$. Menger's first problem asks whether the real line space with the standard angle function is the only angle space that satisfies this independence property for all lines. The second problem seeks a method to calculate the angle between two lines in a way that is linear in the parameters defining those lines. We provide solutions to both of these problems. Specifically, we introduce a new function $\sigma$ that maps pairs of real numbers to the angle between their lines, and then show that the angle between two lines can be calculated as the maximum value of their difference, which is equivalent to finding the angle between their lines as the supremum of $\sigma(r,s)$ over all real numbers $r$ and $s$. This function $\sigma$ satisfies the required properties and provides a way to calculate the angle between two lines in a linear manner. Furthermore, we establish that the standard line space is the only angle space that satisfies the independence property for all lines, and that this property is equivalent to the condition that the function $\sigma$ is affine. Finally, we show that the standard line space is the unique angle space that satisfies this condition and has the property that the angle between two lines is equal to zero if and only if those lines are the same. This last property is not implied by the independence condition, and we provide a counterexample to show that there are angle spaces that do not satisfy it. This counterexample is the set of lines defined by the equation $x-y = 1$ in the plane, where the angle between two lines is defined as the angle between the lines containing those lines and the $x$-axis. This space satisfies the independence condition but does not satisfy the property that the angle between two lines is equal to zero if and only if those lines are the same. This counterexample can be generalized to the space of lines defined by the equation $x-y = t$ in the plane, where the angle between two lines is defined as the angle between the lines containing those lines and the $x$-axis

Furthermore, we show that SparseGAN can be easily integrated into pre-trained language models, such as T5 and BART, without the need for significant modifications. Our research develops two distinct algorithms to estimate the network's size: one that relies on short-range communication and another that utilizes longer-range communication. Both algorithms are robust against a wide range of Byzantine faults and provide accurate size estimates. Furthermore, we establish a key performance metric, known as the additive error, which serves as an indicator of the algorithms' precision. By analyzing the conditions under which the algorithms operate, we derive a non-asymptotic bound for the additive error. Additionally, we compare our algorithms to existing solutions in various network configurations, demonstrating their effectiveness and efficiency. Our research provides a novel approach to resolving the network scale estimation challenge in small-world networks with Byzantine faults. Our algorithms' performance metrics can be used as a benchmark for future research. Our research also offers insights into the optimal network configurations for accurate size estimation. Identifying changes in brain connectivity is crucial for understanding neurological disorders and their progression. However, estimating connectivity from EEG data is challenging due to its high dimensionality and the presence of noise. Traditional methods rely on source separation techniques and graph theory but are often computationally expensive and require precise electrode placement. In contrast, a recent data-driven approach uses autoencoders to estimate connectivity directly from EEG data but is limited in its ability to track changes over time. To address this, we propose a novel method that combines the benefits of both approaches by utilizing a recurrent autoencoder to efficiently capture the dynamic nature of EEG connectivity. To reduce computational costs and improve accuracy, we employ a dimensionality reduction technique and optimize the model using a novel loss function that balances reconstruction and graph Laplacian regularization. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we applied it to a dataset featuring patients with traumatic brain injury and healthy controls, and the resulting connectivity estimates exhibited high correlation with ground truth values and accurately captured changes over time. Biological entities such as animals and plants are ubiquitous in outdoor environments and are frequently observed in video footage. The automatic identification of these entities in video streams is a valuable tool for various applications, including surveillance of invasive species, monitoring of wildlife populations, and assessment of vegetation health. However, the development of accurate and efficient methods for detecting biological movement in videos is hindered by the lack of a universally accepted definition for such movement. This ambiguity is compounded by the diverse range of biological entities, each with its unique characteristics, speeds, and patterns of movement. Furthermore, the presence of biological movement can be subtle, and it often coexists with other visual phenomena like weather conditions, lighting variations, and human activity. In this paper, we present a comprehensive review of the current approaches for detecting biological movement in videos, along with a proposed framework for evaluating such methods. We also outline the key challenges and potential applications in this area. The paper concludes with a discussion of the future directions for research in this field. In 2019, a novel iterative method for matrix inversion was introduced, leveraging a higher-order upwind central (HOU) scheme that demonstrated a 2.5-fold increase in speed over the standard iterative Thomas algorithm when applied to a 3D case. However, this method's potential for further optimization on GPU platforms remained unexplored. In the present study, we refine the original HOU scheme to enhance compatibility with the Thomas algorithm, paving the way for a 2-step iterative matrix inversion process. This process was successfully implemented on a GPU, yielding a 3-fold reduction in computational time for a 3D case. Furthermore, the method's applicability was demonstrated through the numerical solution of the 2D convection-diffusion equation. Additionally, the study delves into the theoretical underpinnings of the HOU scheme, providing a comprehensive framework for this technique's application in various computational contexts. In contextual linear bandits, a learner makes decisions in a sequence of contexts drawn from a unknown distribution, with the goal of minimizing regret. We consider a decentralized setting where multiple agents, each observing a contextual linear reward model, aim to optimize their decisions independently. We establish a lower bound on the cumulative regret of $\\Omega(\\sqrt{d^2K T}\\log N)$ for $d$-dimensional contextual linear bandits with $K$ contexts, where $N$ denotes the number of agents and $T$ the time horizon. We then design a computationally efficient decentralized algorithm, Contextual Linear Distributed Upper Confidence Bound (CLDOBE), which achieves a cumulative regret of $\\tilde{O}(d^2\\sqrt{K T}\\log T + d\\sqrt{K T}\\log^2 T + d\\sqrt{T})$ for an arbitrary context distribution. We further show that CLDOBE attains a cumulative regret of $\\tilde{O}(d^2\\sqrt{T} + d\\sqrt{T K}\\log T + d\\sqrt{T K}\\log^2 T)$ when the context distribution is uniform over $K$ contexts. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our decentralized algorithm through numerical experiments. Our results provide a lower bound and an algorithm for the general contextual linear bandit setting with multiple agents, as well as a sharper upper bound for the uniform context distribution case. We also discuss the connection to the centralized contextual linear bandit problem. We further investigate the decentralized linear bandit problem with a single agent and multiple contexts, obtaining a lower bound of $\\Omega(\\sqrt{d^2K T}\\log T)$ and designing an algorithm with a cumulative regret of $\\tilde{O}(d^2\\sqrt{K T}\\log T + d\\sqrt{K T}\\log^2 T)$. The study of cometary spectra containing molecular cations is crucial for understanding the composition of cometary gas and the formation of solar system material. However, the analysis of these spectra is hindered by the limited availability of theoretical and laboratory data, particularly for cations of the most abundant elements like oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen. This study aims to highlight the existing knowledge gaps in the spectra of oxygen-containing molecular cations, which are critical for interpreting the spectral features of comets like C/2013 A1 (Siding Spring) and 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. By examining the existing literature and laboratory experiments, the research reveals that there are significant gaps in the spectral data for many of these cations, particularly in the far-ultraviolet range, which is essential for analyzing the spectra of cometary gas. To overcome these limitations, the study proposes potential avenues for future research, including laboratory experiments and theoretical calculations that can provide the necessary spectral information for a more comprehensive understanding of cometary composition. By addressing these knowledge gaps, the study can provide a more accurate and detailed picture of the solar system's early formation and the evolution of the outer planets.

As machine learning models become increasingly widespread, there's a growing need to develop privacy-preserving and decentralized learning methods that can effectively utilize data from diverse sources. However, learning from such data faces significant challenges due to its inherent heterogeneity, which causes difficulties in optimizing models and degrades their performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel random walk-based approach for learning from heterogeneous data in a decentralized manner. This method enables agents to explore the data space efficiently, visit more representative data points, and produce high-quality models that generalize well to unseen areas. Through extensive simulations and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional methods in various scenarios, including those with non-stationary environments and complex graphs. Furthermore, our approach is scalable and can be applied to real-world problems, as evidenced by our study using a large-scale real-world dataset. We also provide a theoretical guarantee for the convergence of our algorithm, which serves as a foundation for future optimization techniques. Our approach and associated code are publicly available on GitHub.

Consider a mixture model where observations are generated from one of several distributions, each associated with a specific component. The distribution of the observed data is then modeled as a mixture of these components, with the respective mixing weights determining the probability of selecting each distribution. The task at hand is to estimate the weighted average of the model parameters given a sample of observations. A key challenge arises when the number of observations exceeds the number of components, as the weighted average of the parameters is no longer identifiable without additional assumptions. A Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimator (GMLE) is proposed to estimate the weighted average of the model parameters under various distributional scenarios, including exponential family distributions and their applications in sampling designs. Theoretical properties of the GMLE are established, and its efficacy is demonstrated through simulations and real-world examples, including the estimation of population totals in sampling designs. The proposed method is shown to be particularly effective when the sample size exceeds the number of components. The GMLE is also found to be robust to misspecification of the distribution of the components. The R package'mixGAM' is available for implementing the GMLE in various scenarios. The methodological contributions of this research are further illustrated through the development of a Generalized Expectation Maximization (GEM) algorithm for estimating the parameters of the Dirichlet process mixture model, as well as the application of the GMLE to the estimation of the weighted average of model parameters in sampling designs. The efficacy of the GMLE is also demonstrated through the estimation of the population total in sampling designs. The research is concluded by discussing the potential applications of the GMLE in other fields. The paper is accompanied by supplementary materials. As the number of mobile devices participating in federated learning grows, optimizing communication efficiency becomes increasingly important. To minimize communication, many systems use asynchronous aggregation, where a central server combines model updates received from devices at their leisure. However, this approach can lead to performance issues due to the unrestricted use of gradient descent without bounds on the norm of the update vectors. To address this challenge, researchers have explored various methods to constrain gradients, but these approaches often require significant computational resources and cannot handle large-scale systems with many participating devices. In contrast, we propose a simple and efficient method called buffered asynchronous aggregation without constraints, where the server stores a history of model updates and combines them asynchronously, without imposing limits on the gradient descent method used by devices. We derive a theoretical performance guarantee for this approach and demonstrate its practical effectiveness through large-scale experiments using real-world datasets. Our results show that this method achieves comparable performance to constrained methods while reducing communication overhead by up to 50 times. To further improve performance, we also introduce a novel method called asynchronous aggregation with delayed participation, where devices can join or leave the system at their leisure. Our findings provide a performance-cost tradeoff for the proposed methods and offer practical guidelines for optimizing communication efficiency in large-scale federated learning systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengwuxx/Fed-AGG.

To enhance speech recognition systems, a common approach is to incorporate pre-trained language models through multi-task learning. However, training such a system from scratch for a new language can be challenging due to the need for large amounts of labeled data. To address this issue, researchers have explored transfer learning methods using existing models trained on similar languages. In this paper, we investigate the application of transfer learning to systems that have already been trained and are highly accurate. Our experiments involve fine-tuning a state-of-the-art speech recognition system trained on English to recognize spoken words in French. The findings show that even without additional labeled data, the system can be further improved by training a small set of parameters on English monophones. When combined with unsupervised adaptation, the system achieves a significant 8.6% relative improvement in recognition accuracy. Furthermore, we explore the use of transfer learning to recognize accented English and find that it is also effective. The system can be easily adapted to new languages by simply replacing the language model, without the need for additional training or labeled data. The code is available at https://github.com/GoogleCloudSpeechToText/ctf_ctlang_asr_transfer.

In situations where a robot operates in a dynamic environment with limited visibility, a guidance system is crucial to ensure its safe navigation. We propose a novel TD-learning method that combines Gaussian Process regression and sparse updates to guide a robot through a complex underwater environment. This approach addresses the challenges of TD-learning in dynamic environments by efficiently updating the value function using sparse Gaussian Process interpolation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by conducting experiments on a simulated underwater scenario, and the results show that our approach outperforms traditional TD-learning methods in both exploration and navigation phases. Additionally, we apply the proposed method to a real-world underwater robot guidance problem, and the results confirm that our approach is practical and efficient for guiding a robot in a dynamic underwater environment. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yang/GP_TD.

Linguistic standardization is crucial for enabling effective communication, and a significant amount of effort has been invested in creating language resources, such as dictionaries and style guides, to facilitate this process. However, these resources are not universally applicable and may vary greatly across languages, dialects, and genres. As a result, standardization is typically performed manually, requiring substantial time and resources. In this research, we present a novel approach to standardizing linguistic content automatically, focusing on grammatical error correction. Our method employs a few examples to adapt a correction model across domains, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments conducted on the English TreeBank and the Grammatical Error Correction (GCC) corpus. The results show that our approach achieves superior performance when adapting to new domains with limited data, surpassing the performance of a strong baseline by 10.3% in terms of F-score. Furthermore, we introduce a novel evaluation metric to assess the standardization of linguistic content, and our approach ranks 2nd in the 2020 GCC shared task. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/Meta-Standardizer.

In a setting where agents have private preferences for indivisible goods and may act strategically, we investigate the existence of a Nash equilibrium under various allocation rules. Our primary focus is on the proportional allocation rule, which prioritizes fairness by allocating goods in proportion to the value an agent places on having any good. We examine the conditions under which a Nash equilibrium exists for all possible preference profiles. Our study reveals that the existence of a Nash equilibrium is guaranteed if preferences are single-peaked, but there are instances where no pure Nash equilibrium exists for single-parameter preferences. We also explore the relationship between the value of a Nash equilibrium and the value an agent would achieve in a fair allocation under truthful reporting. Our findings demonstrate that the proportionate allocation rule ensures that the value of a Nash equilibrium is at least one-third of the value achieved under truthful reporting. Furthermore, we examine the impact of side payments on the existence of a Nash equilibrium and the associated costs. Our research also delves into the connection between the proportionate allocation rule and other mechanisms, such as the random serial dictatorship, as well as the role of fairness in the context of large societies. Our study highlights the significance of considering the strategic behavior of agents in the context of allocating indivisible goods and the importance of examining the conditions under which mechanisms like the proportionate allocation rule are robust against self-interested agents. Our findings also demonstrate that the proportionate allocation rule is a 'good' mechanism even in non-cooperative settings, as it provides a high level of fairness and achieves a good level of efficiency at a relatively low cost. Offline learning for multiple agents in a shared environment is challenging due to the interdependence of their actions, which requires a significant amount of data to train effectively. Current approaches often rely on data that is uniformly high-quality, but this is impractical in real-world scenarios. Instead, we propose a method to train multiple offline agents using data with varying levels of quality, by selectively learning from successful trajectories. This is achieved by introducing a dual-training framework that simultaneously refines the policy and corrects the bias in the data distribution. The policy is updated to prioritize actions that are likely to succeed in similar situations, while the data bias is corrected to account for the diversity of successful experiences. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on offline multi-agent reinforcement learning, using both simulated and real-world data. The resulting method is simple yet powerful, and can handle complex tasks involving multiple agents, as well as those with a single decision-maker. We also provide a Python implementation of the method.

The proliferation of visually rich documents like receipts, invoices, and medical records necessitates the development of automatic extraction models to streamline data processing. However, the high cost of manually labeling these documents for training accurate models poses a significant barrier. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach to reduce labeling costs by more than 99% for a range of visually rich document extraction tasks. Our method involves training a high-performing extraction model on a small set of labeled documents, and then fine-tunes it using a diverse set of unlabeled documents with minimal annotations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in multiple document extraction tasks, including extracting information from receipts, invoices, and medical records, with a significant decrease in labeling costs. Furthermore, our method allows for the incorporation of external knowledge to enhance model performance. We have made our code and data publicly available to facilitate future research and development.

The growing need to utilize large amounts of memory in deep learning applications has led to increased interest in object-based programming for GPUs. In response, researchers have proposed various methods to optimize memory allocation, yet these approaches often prioritize speed over safety and may result in unpredictable performance. To address this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed to balance security and efficiency while utilizing up to 32 threads. Our system employs a novel hybrid allocation strategy that combines a hierarchical free list with a block-based approach to minimize fragmentation and accelerate memory allocation. Furthermore, DynaSOAr includes a memory access predictor to optimize memory allocation based on access patterns and a cache-aware allocator to reduce cache conflicts. In our evaluation, DynaSOAr demonstrates improved performance and lower fragmentation compared to existing methods, while also exhibiting strong scalability. When applied to real-world deep learning workloads, DynaSOAr achieves a 1.5x to 2.5x speedup over the NVIDIA CUDA Dynamic Global Memory Allocator. Our findings also reveal that DynaSOAr's memory access predictor and cache-aware allocator contribute significantly to its performance gains. To facilitate further research, we have made DynaSOAr's source code publicly available.

In neural machine translation, the focus mechanism enables the model to selectively concentrate on specific input elements when generating output. However, this approach typically relies on the model to focus on the same elements as the target output, which may not always be desirable. We introduce a novel look-ahead focus mechanism that allows the model to focus on different input elements than the target output, providing a more flexible way to handle complex relationships between inputs and outputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on several translation tasks, showing that it outperforms the standard focus mechanism and other baselines. Moreover, we find that it can be viewed as a form of multi-head attention, and it is particularly beneficial for handling situations with multiple, conflicting relationships between inputs and outputs. We also examine the model's behavior to gain insights into its performance. Our method is simple to implement and can be applied to other sequence-to-sequence tasks. We release our code and pre-trained models for public use.

The Vector Boson Approximation (VBA) has been a widely used tool in electroweak theory for high-energy particle collisions, particularly effective in describing $WW$ and $WZ/W\gamma$ scattering processes. This approximation is particularly advantageous for calculations involving high-energy processes at future high-energy lepton colliders, such as the Future Circular Lepton Collider (FCC), due to its computational efficiency. In this study, we examine the VBA's applicability and accuracy in calculating scattering processes involving vector bosons at the FCC muon collider, with a focus on the 1.5 TeV and 3.0 TeV energy levels. We also explore the VBA's limitations and potential improvements by examining the effects of higher-order corrections and the role of QCD interactions. Furthermore, this research aims to provide a foundation for developing efficient VBA-based methods to calculate scattering processes at the FCC muon collider.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents can excel across a wide range of
tasks by leveraging their shared underlying structure. However, a significant issue
emerges when agents are faced with a diverse set of tasks in a single environment:
catastrophic interference between tasks. This phenomenon causes the agent to
rapidly forget previously learned skills when it encounters new tasks, hindering
its ability to generalize effectively. To address this challenge, we propose a
modular network architecture that enables the agent to learn a wide range of
tasks without interference. Our approach utilizes separate policy networks for
each task, which are combined through a modular controller. By applying policy
regularization and a modular controller that prioritizes exploration, our system
demonstrates superior performance in diverse settings. Furthermore, we introduce a
new evaluation metric, known as the generalization loss, to assess the agent's
ability to generalize across tasks. Our modular network architecture excels in
both sparse and dense reward settings, as evidenced by our comprehensive
experiments. Ultimately, our findings provide valuable insights into the design
of future multi-task reinforcement learning systems capable of generalizing across
a wide range of tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChengtingHuang/Modular-MT-RL.

To address this, we developed the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, an end-to-end, raw waveform generative model that combines the expanded convolutional neural network and WaveNet architectures to efficiently capture both local and long-range periodic patterns in speech. This model's unique design enables it to automatically learn the quasi-periodic characteristics of speech without requiring external pitch features. To accommodate a wide range of pitch periods, we introduced a dynamic dilation pattern that allows for seamless expansion and contraction of the convolutional neural network. To further enhance performance, we developed a novel training method called pitch-dependent expanded convolution, which optimizes the model's performance for different pitch ranges. Experimental results demonstrate the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet's superiority over existing methods in terms of naturalness and subjective quality evaluations. By utilizing the coefficients of the underlying geometry, L-GNN learns node representations that are invariant to the graph's topological structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method on several classification tasks, including those involving graphs with topological inconsistencies, and show that L-GNN outperforms state-of-the-art GNN baselines. Moreover, we apply L-GNN to learn node embeddings on a real-world citation network and visualize the resulting embeddings to obtain valuable insights.
